title: License Plate Optical Tracking Networks: Movement as Record
body:
The GLMZ License Plate Optical Tracking Network, administered jointly by the Municipal Transit Authority and the Corponation Security Consortium under the 2179 Unified Mobility Surveillance Accord, comprises approximately 340,000 fixed optical readers distributed across road infrastructure, tunnel chokepoints, parking structures, and elevated transit corridors throughout the city's inhabited zones. Each reader captures high-resolution imagery at up to 240 frames per second, extracting alphanumeric plate data alongside vehicle silhouette geometry, occupant count estimates derived from thermal overlay, and chassis color and modification profiles. Reads are timestamped to millisecond precision and uploaded to the Meridian Mobility Intelligence Repository within 1.2 seconds of capture, where they are retained in hot storage for 18 months and cold archive for a mandatory minimum of seven years under city charter.

The system processes approximately 4.2 billion plate reads per day across all vehicle classes, from registered personal transports to commercial freight convoys to the unregistered improvised vehicles common in Periphery districts. Unregistered vehicles trigger immediate anomaly flags rather than identity matches, generating location-tagged unknown vehicle events that are routed to district security contractors for manual review or autonomous drone dispatch depending on zone classification. The tracking network integrates with the Ambient Sensor Mesh to triangulate vehicle positions even when plates are obscured, using chassis geometry fingerprinting and exhaust thermal signature matching as supplementary identification vectors. Journey reconstruction algorithms can generate complete movement histories for any registered vehicle with greater than 94% spatial accuracy across the monitored zone network.

The legal framework governing plate tracking data is among the most contested in GLMZ surveillance law. Corporate zones treat vehicle movement data as employer-accessible information when the vehicle is company-registered, allowing fleet tracking and after-hours monitoring of vehicles provided as employment benefits. Municipal zones nominally restrict access to law enforcement and licensed security contractors, but data-sharing agreements with 23 corporate entities create effective open access for any organization with a Tier 2 or above Municipal Partnership License. Civil liberties collectives in the Academic Enclave have documented cases in which plate tracking data was used to establish proof of presence at labor organizing meetings, subsequently used as grounds for indenture contract termination. The admissibility of such data in corporate arbitration hearings was upheld in three separate 2182 Meridian Arbitration Panel rulings.

Countermeasures against plate tracking form a significant informal economy in Periphery and Undercroft districts. Thermochromic plate coatings that shift alphanumeric rendering under specific temperature conditions, retroreflective blocking sprays that saturate optical sensors at acute angles, and entirely fabricated ghost plates registered to dissolved corporate shells are all commercially available through gray market channels. The Municipal Transit Authority estimates that between 8 and 14 percent of vehicles in Periphery districts are operating with some form of plate countermeasure at any given time. Detection of countermeasure use triggers automatic escalation to a Class 2 Municipal Violation, carrying fines calibrated to assessed income level — a calculation that is itself derived from platform data, creating a circular enforcement architecture that critics describe as a poverty trap.
